rounds.hypothesis: PR_SET_NAME uses read_cstring, which rejects over-long names with ENAMETOOLONG. Linux instead uses strncpy_from_user, which silently truncates to the first 15 bytes and returns success. The 18-byte name 'prctl05_test_xxxxx' triggers this: Asterinas returns -1/ENAMETOOLONG at the first syscall in tcase 2, while Linux truncates it to 'prctl05_test_xx' and returns 0.
rounds.change: Added CurrentUserSpace::read_cstring_truncated, a sibling to read_cstring that matches Linux's strncpy_from_user semantics: returns at most max_len-1 bytes, reporting an error only if the string is unreadable (EFAULT), never for over-length. It reads exactly max_len-1 bytes from user space (matching Linux's count argument), preserving the lowerbound check and address-space clamping that read_cstring implements. Changed sys_prctl's PR_SET_NAME arm to call read_cstring_truncated instead of read_cstring. Enabled prctl05 in all.txt by uncommenting line 1108.
rounds.outcome: green: prctl05 passed 8/8 assertions. Both tcases now pass: tcase 1 ('prctl05_test', 12 bytes) and tcase 2 ('prctl05_test_xxxxx', 18 bytes) both return success from PR_SET_NAME. The stored name is truncated to 15 bytes as expected ('prctl05_test_xx' for tcase 2), and PR_GET_NAME, /proc/self/comm, and /proc/self/task/<tid>/comm all read the correct value. Test output: 'Suite: syscalls / prctl05: pass (0.014s) / Results: Passed: 8 / All conformance tests passed.'

layer: The syscall-entry argument-marshalling layer, as diagnosed. Specifically, the PR_SET_NAME arm of sys_prctl in kernel/src/syscall/prctl.rs, which now chooses a truncating user-space string reader (read_cstring_truncated) instead of the reject-on-overflow one (read_cstring). The truncation-enforcement layer itself — ThreadName::set_name_as_bytes in kernel/src/process/posix_thread/name.rs — was already correct and remains untouched. This is the two-level split diagnosed: the entry decides that over-length is legal; the field decides where the cut lands. To provide the truncating reader, a new method was added to CurrentUserSpace (kernel/src/context.rs) alongside read_cstring. This addition does not change read_cstring's behavior, so all 52 existing callers remain unaffected.
generalizes: The fix is correct for all callers because there is only one: sys_prctl's PR_SET_NAME arm is the sole place in the tree where a thread name is read from user space (grep for MAX_THREAD_NAME_LEN / set_name confirms this). The test exercises two boundaries: a 12-byte name (within limit) and an 18-byte name (over limit). The fix handles both, and also generalizes to: (1) names of exactly 15 bytes (the 16th byte is the nul; Linux reads exactly 15 and succeeds; Asterinas now reads 15 via read_cstring_truncated's max_len-1 window and succeeds); (2) unreadable addresses (NULL or unmapped), which propagate EFAULT as before; (3) names placed near the top of the user address space, where the new method's address-space clamping (inherited from read_cstring's design) ensures Linux-faithful behavior. The truncating semantics are specific to PR_SET_NAME and do not affect any other prctl command or any other use of read_cstring. The one future caller is write(2) to /proc/[pid]/comm, which is currently unimplemented (returns EOPNOTSUPP) but will need identical truncating semantics when someone implements it; read_cstring_truncated is the primitive that caller will use. This is not a special case for the test; it is the correct implementation of Linux's prctl(PR_SET_NAME) semantics.
fix_summary: Added CurrentUserSpace::read_cstring_truncated, a new public method in kernel/src/context.rs that matches Linux's strncpy_from_user: it reads at most max_len-1 bytes from user space and returns them as a C string, reporting an error only if the string is unreadable (EFAULT), never for over-length. The method reuses read_cstring's careful address handling: the lowerbound check (EFAULT for NULL with no page fault), the address-space clamp (EFAULT when the string runs off the top of user space), and delegation to read_cstring_until_end (which appends a nul byte when none is found, yielding a truncated result). This is designed against Asterinas's existing abstractions — read_cstring is the reject-on-overflow sibling for paths, read_cstring_truncated is the truncate-on-overflow sibling for fixed-size name fields — rather than duplicating logic at each call site. Changed sys_prctl's PR_SET_NAME arm to call read_cstring_truncated instead of read_cstring. Enabled prctl05 in test/initramfs/src/conformance/ltp/testcases/all.txt. The fix went green on the first attempt.
